t.1.73.2: Then all of them, having assembled together, said to Śatakratu: "Now is the time for your valor; slay the enemies, O Puraṃdara!"
t.1.73.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: When Kaca, having mastered the knowledge, had arrived, the dwellers of heaven were overjoyed; having learned that knowledge from Kaca, they had achieved their purpose, O bull of the Bharatas.
t.1.73.3: Thus addressed by the assembled thirty gods, Maghavan then said, "So be it," and set out; in the forest he saw some women.
t.1.73.4: While the maidens were playing in a forest like Caitraratha, he, having become the wind, mixed up all of their garments.
t.1.73.5: Then those maidens, coming up together out of the water, seized the garments, each taking whichever lay nearest, in a confused mix.
t.1.73.6: Then Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, took Devayānī's garment there, not knowing that the clothes had been mixed up.
t.1.73.7: Then, O king of kings, a quarrel arose there between the two of them, Devayānī and Śarmiṣṭhā, on account of that.
t.1.73.8: Why do you take my garment, Asurī, when you are my pupil? For you, who are devoid of proper conduct, no good will come.
t.1.73.9: Your father, standing low like a humble servant, constantly praises and salutes my father, whether he is seated or lying down.
t.1.73.10: For you are the daughter of one who begs, who praises, and who accepts gifts; I am the daughter of one who is praised, who gives, and who does not accept.
t.1.73.11: Unarmed against one who is armed, empty-handed, you rage, beggar-girl! You will meet one who fights back, for I do not count you as anything at all.
t.1.73.13: Thinking, "She is dead," Śarmiṣṭhā, whose intent was wicked, went home without looking back, wholly given over to the force of her anger.
t.1.73.12: As Devayānī rose up and clung to the garment, Śarmiṣṭhā threw her into a well, and then she returned to her own city.
t.1.73.14: Then Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, came to that place, hunting for deer, thirsty, his draught animals weary and his horses weary.
t.1.73.15: That son of Nahuṣa, Nāhuṣa, looking into the well whose water was gone, saw there that maiden, blazing like a tongue of fire.
t.1.73.16: As soon as he saw that maiden of divine complexion, the best of kings comforted her with exceedingly gentle, conciliatory words and questioned her.
t.1.73.18: And how did you fall into this well covered with creepers and grass? And whose daughter are you? Tell me everything, O slender-waisted one.
t.1.73.17: Who are you, dark lady with copper-red nails and earrings of polished jewels? You brood long and deeply; and why do you sigh so, distressed?
t.1.73.20: Here, O king, is my right hand, with its copper-red nails and fingers; take hold of me and lift me out, for I deem you to be of noble birth.
t.1.73.19: I am the daughter of that Śukra who by his knowledge raises up the Daityas slain by the gods; surely he does not know what has become of me.
t.1.73.21: For I know you to be calm, valorous, and renowned; therefore you ought to lift me out of this well into which I have fallen.
t.1.73.22: Then the son of Nahuṣa, recognizing her as a woman and a brahmin, took her by the right hand and lifted her out of the pit.
t.1.73.23: And having swiftly drawn her out of that well, King Yayāti took leave of the fair-hipped maiden and went to his own city.
t.1.73.24: Go quickly, Ghūrṇikā, and tell my father everything, for I will not now enter the city of Vṛṣaparvan.
t.1.73.26: I tell you, O greatly wise one, O illustrious one: Devayānī has been struck down in the forest by Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan.
t.1.73.25: Ghūrṇikā went swiftly to the palace of the Asura, and on seeing Kāvya she spoke these words, her mind seized with alarm.
t.1.73.27: Having heard that his daughter had been struck down there by Śarmiṣṭhā, Kāvya went out in haste, out of grief, searching for his daughter in the forest.
t.1.73.28: Then Kāvya, seeing his daughter Devayānī in the forest, embraced her with both arms and, grief-stricken, spoke these words.
t.1.73.30: Whether there be amends for me or not, listen attentively to what I was told by Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan. She said this, and it is true indeed: 'You are the singer of the Daityas.'
t.1.73.29: All people are bound to sorrow and happiness by their own faults; I think there is some misdeed of yours, for which this atonement has been made.
t.1.73.31: For thus does Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, speak to me, uttering words sharp and harsh, her eyes deeply reddened with rage.
t.1.73.32: For you are the daughter of one who praises, who begs, and who accepts gifts; I am the daughter of one who is praised, who gives, and who does not accept.
t.1.73.33: Thus Śarmiṣṭhā, the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, spoke to me again and again, her eyes reddened with anger, full of pride.
t.1.73.35: Śukra said: You are not the daughter of one who praises, good lady, nor of one who receives; you are the daughter of one who does not praise but is himself praised, Devayānī.
t.1.73.34: "If I am indeed the daughter of one who sings praises and accepts gifts, father, then I shall seek to appease Śarmiṣṭhā": thus was my friend told by me.
t.1.73.36: Vṛṣaparvan himself knows this, as do Śakra and King Nāhuṣa: my power is the inconceivable brahman, beyond all pairs of opposites, truly sovereign.
